questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 508 B?
options: A Brief Foundations mathematics course in Anderson Engineering: an overview and six lectures, about an hour
An optional elective outside the Foundations
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour.
C is wrong: It is a Foundations course.
D is wrong: It is a lecture course.

questions.q: What is the backbone of this course?
options: MIT OpenCourseWare 18.06SC Linear Algebra, taught by Professor Gilbert Strang
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.9: The overview credits Professor Strang.
A is wrong: That backs Differential Equations.
C is wrong: That backs Calculus Two.
D is wrong: That backs Probability and Statistics.

Paragraph 1.2: Vectors add component by component.
A is wrong: That multiplies components.
B is wrong: That adds all entries.
C is wrong: That subtracts.

questions.q: What do all linear combinations of two non-parallel vectors in three dimensions fill?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.3: One vector fills a line; three independent vectors fill space.
B is wrong: That is one vector.
C is wrong: That needs three independent vectors.
D is wrong: Combinations sweep out a plane.

questions.q: What is the dot product of (1, 2) and (3, 4)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.4: 1·3 + 2·4 = 11.
B is wrong: The dot product is a number, not a vector.
C is wrong: That is the sum of all entries.
D is wrong: That is the length of (3, 4).

questions.q: What is the length of (3, 4)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.4: √(3² + 4²) = 5.
A is wrong: That adds the components.
B is wrong: That is the squared length.
D is wrong: That multiplies the components.

questions.q: In the column way of computing A x, what is A x?
options: The dot product of x with itself
A linear combination of the columns of A, weighted by the components of x
The rows of A added together
A matrix the same size as A
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: The row way takes dot products of rows with x.
A is wrong: That is the squared length of x.
C is wrong: The weights come from x.
D is wrong: A x is a vector.

questions.q: What solves 2x − y = 0 and −x + 2y = 3?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.7: The two lines meet at (1, 2): 2 − 2 = 0 and −1 + 4 = 3.
A is wrong: 2·2 − 1 ≠ 0.
B is wrong: The second equation fails.
C is wrong: The second equation gives 1, not 3.

questions.q: In the column picture of 2x − y = 0, −x + 2y = 3, which combination of the columns (2, −1) and (−1, 2) gives (0, 3)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: (2 − 2, −1 + 4) = (0, 3).
A is wrong: That gives (3, 0).
B is wrong: That gives (1, 1).
C is wrong: The matrix is invertible.

questions.q: If a 2 × 2 matrix has columns (1, 2) and (2, 4), when does A x = b have a solution?
options: Only when b lies on the line through (1, 2), and then infinitely many
Exactly two solutions for every b
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.10: The second column is twice the first, so the matrix is singular.
B is wrong: That needs independent columns.
C is wrong: b on the line gives solutions.
D is wrong: Linear systems never have exactly two.

questions.q: What makes a matrix transformation linear?
options: It maps every vector to zero
A(x + y) = Ax + Ay and A(cx) = c Ax
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: Matrices can rotate, stretch, reflect, or shear the plane.
A is wrong: That is one linear map, not the definition.
C is wrong: Only orthogonal matrices do.
D is wrong: Linearity adds outputs.

questions.q: What does the identity matrix do to a vector?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.13: It has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.
B is wrong: That is 2I.
C is wrong: That is −I.
D is wrong: That is the zero matrix.

questions.q: Solve x + 2y = 3, 3x + 8y = 5 by elimination.
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.2: Subtracting 3 × row 1 gives 2y = −4; then x = 3 − 2(−2) = 7.
A is wrong: That fails the second equation.
B is wrong: Back substitution gives y = −2.
D is wrong: That fails both equations.

questions.q: What happens if elimination finds a zero pivot that no row exchange can fix?
options: The system has exactly one solution
The matrix is singular: no solution or infinitely many
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: On a computer, partial pivoting also chooses large pivots for accuracy.
A is wrong: Singularity does not imply x = 0.
B is wrong: Unique solutions need n pivots.
C is wrong: A singular matrix has determinant zero.

questions.q: When is the product A B defined?
options: When A and B are the same size
When the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.5: Entry (i, j) is row i of A dotted with column j of B.
A is wrong: Square matrices of equal size are one case only.
B is wrong: Rectangular products are allowed.
C is wrong: Shapes must match.

questions.q: In A = L U, what does L contain?
options: Ones on its diagonal and the elimination multipliers below it
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: U is the upper triangular result of elimination.
B is wrong: The pivots are on U's diagonal.
C is wrong: L is not A⁻¹.
D is wrong: Eigenvalues are unrelated to L U.

questions.q: Why does software factor a matrix once and reuse the factors?
options: Factoring is cheaper than any solve
Factoring costs about n³, but each new right-hand side then costs only about n²
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: Structures are often analysed for hundreds of load cases.
A is wrong: Sparsity is a separate matter.
B is wrong: Factoring is the expensive step.
C is wrong: Factors avoid computing the inverse.

questions.q: What is (A B)⁻¹?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.10: Like socks and shoes, undo in reverse order.
A is wrong: The order reverses.
C is wrong: That is not true.
D is wrong: That is the product, not its inverse.

questions.q: What is (A B)ᵀ?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: The transpose of a product reverses the order.
B is wrong: The order reverses.
C is wrong: Transposing changes the matrix.
D is wrong: Transposes are needed.

questions.q: What kind of matrix is RᵀR for any R?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.12: Its transpose is RᵀR again.
A is wrong: Not in general.
C is wrong: Not in general.
D is wrong: Only if R has orthonormal columns.

questions.q: Why are most large engineering matrices sparse?
options: Each unknown interacts with only a few neighbours
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.13: A finite-element model may have only a few dozen non-zeros per row.
A is wrong: Structure, not randomness, causes sparsity.
C is wrong: They are large.
D is wrong: Sparsity is about zeros in entries.

questions.q: When does A x = b have a solution?
options: Exactly when b is in the column space of A
Exactly when b is in the nullspace
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.2: The column space contains all combinations of the columns.
B is wrong: The nullspace concerns A x = 0.
C is wrong: Not when b lies outside C(A).
D is wrong: Many non-zero b work.

questions.q: What is the complete solution of A x = b, when one exists?
options: Any vector in the column space
A particular solution plus any vector in the nullspace
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: The nullspace part solves A x = 0 and adds nothing to b.
A is wrong: That solves A x = 0.
B is wrong: The column space is in the output space.
D is wrong: Nullspace vectors may be added.

questions.q: When are vectors linearly independent?
options: When they all have length one
When they are all perpendicular to (1, 1, …, 1)
When at least one is zero
When the only combination giving zero has all weights zero
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.6: No vector is a combination of the others.
A is wrong: Length is irrelevant.
B is wrong: That is unrelated.
C is wrong: Then they are dependent.

questions.q: What is a basis?
options: An independent set of vectors that spans the space
A set of perpendicular vectors only
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.7: Every basis of a space has the same number of vectors, its dimension.
A is wrong: It must also be independent.
B is wrong: It must also span.
D is wrong: Orthogonality is not required.

questions.q: Which of these equals the rank of a matrix?
options: The number of pivots, which equals the number of independent columns and of independent rows
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.8: Rank is the true size of a matrix.
A is wrong: Only if the rows are independent.
B is wrong: Entries do not determine rank this way.
D is wrong: The determinant is a number, possibly zero.

questions.q: For an m × n matrix of rank r, what is the dimension of the nullspace?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: There are n − r free variables.
A is wrong: That is the left nullspace.
B is wrong: That is the row and column space dimension.
D is wrong: Dimensions cannot exceed n.

questions.q: Which two fundamental subspaces lie in Rⁿ for an m × n matrix?
options: The column space and the left nullspace
The column space and the nullspace
The row space and the nullspace
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.10: The column space and left nullspace lie in Rᵐ.
A is wrong: Those lie in Rᵐ.
B is wrong: They live in different spaces.
C is wrong: The nullspace is also in Rⁿ.

questions.q: What is the dimension of the space of polynomials of degree at most three?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.13: A basis is 1, x, x², x³.
A is wrong: The constant term adds one.
B is wrong: The degree is bounded.
D is wrong: Many independent polynomials exist.

questions.q: What is the projection of b onto the line through a?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.2: The error b − p is perpendicular to a.
A is wrong: The direction is a.
B is wrong: The length must be scaled.
D is wrong: That is a number, not a vector.

questions.q: What are the normal equations for projecting b onto the column space of A?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.3: The error b − A x̂ must be perpendicular to every column of A.
A is wrong: That usually has no exact solution.
C is wrong: The product is AᵀA.
D is wrong: That holds only with orthonormal columns.

questions.q: Which two properties characterise a projection matrix P?
options: P is invertible and P² = I
P is symmetric and P² = P
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Projecting a second time changes nothing.
A is wrong: That describes a reflection.
B is wrong: The zero matrix is a trivial projection only.
C is wrong: Orthogonal matrices preserve length; projections usually shorten.

questions.q: For data b = (6, 0, 0) at t = 0, 1, 2, what is the least-squares line?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.6: The normal equations give C = 5 and D = −3, with errors (1, −2, 1).
A is wrong: That does not satisfy the normal equations.
B is wrong: That is only the mean.
C is wrong: That fits only the first two points.

questions.q: What is the inverse of a square orthogonal matrix Q?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: QᵀQ = I, and multiplying by Q preserves lengths and angles.
B is wrong: Only for reflections.
C is wrong: Orthogonal matrices are invertible.
D is wrong: That is not true in general.

questions.q: With orthonormal columns Q, what is the least-squares solution?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.9: QᵀQ = I collapses the normal equations.
B is wrong: The transpose is needed.
C is wrong: QQᵀ is generally singular.
D is wrong: Not in general.

questions.q: What does Gram-Schmidt produce when recorded as a factorisation?
options: A = Q R, with orthonormal Q and upper triangular R
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.11: Least squares becomes R x̂ = Qᵀb.
A is wrong: That records elimination.
C is wrong: That is diagonalisation.
D is wrong: That is the SVD.

questions.q: What does exchanging two rows do to a determinant?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.2: This is one of the three defining properties.
A is wrong: The magnitude is unchanged.
B is wrong: Subtracting a multiple of a row leaves it unchanged; exchange flips sign.
D is wrong: Only if the rows are equal.

questions.q: What is det(A B)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: Also det Aᵀ = det A and det A⁻¹ = 1/det A.
A is wrong: Determinants multiply.
C is wrong: They multiply.
D is wrong: Not in general.

questions.q: How are eigenvalues found?
options: As the diagonal entries of any matrix
As roots of det(A − λI) = 0, the characteristic polynomial
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.5: A − λI must be singular for a non-zero eigenvector.
A is wrong: Only for triangular matrices.
C is wrong: Pivots are generally different.
D is wrong: Columns are vectors, not eigenvalues.

questions.q: What are the eigenvalues of the matrix with rows (2, 1) and (1, 2)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.6: λ² − 4λ + 3 = 0, with eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, −1).
A is wrong: Those are the diagonal entries.
B is wrong: The product must be det = 3.
C is wrong: The sum must be the trace, 4.

questions.q: What is the sum of the eigenvalues of a matrix?
options: Its trace, the sum of the diagonal entries
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.7: The product equals the determinant.
A is wrong: That is the product.
B is wrong: Rank counts pivots.
D is wrong: Not in general.

questions.q: If every eigenvalue of A has size less than one, what happens to Aᵏ as k grows?
options: It equals A for all k
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.9: Aᵏ = X Λᵏ X⁻¹, and each λᵏ → 0.
B is wrong: That needs some |λ| > 1.
C is wrong: Not in general.
D is wrong: That needs all λ = 1.

questions.q: Which eigenvalue does every Markov matrix have?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.11: Its eigenvector gives the steady state.
A is wrong: Not necessarily.
B is wrong: Not necessarily.
D is wrong: Columns sum to one, so λ = 1.

questions.q: What does the spectral theorem say about a real symmetric matrix?
options: It has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors: S = Q Λ Qᵀ
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.1: It acts by rotating, stretching along axes, and rotating back.
B is wrong: They are all real.
C is wrong: It always can.
D is wrong: Its eigenvalues vary.

questions.q: Which test shows a symmetric matrix S is positive definite?
options: xᵀ S x > 0 for every non-zero x
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: Equivalently all eigenvalues, pivots, or upper-left determinants are positive.
B is wrong: Positive entries are not sufficient.
C is wrong: Positive determinant alone is not enough.
D is wrong: Diagonal matrices can have negative entries.

questions.q: What is the Cholesky factorisation?
options: S = L Lᵀ for a positive definite S, about twice as fast as general L U
S = L U with any L
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.5: Positive definite matrices need no row exchanges.
A is wrong: That is Gram-Schmidt.
B is wrong: That is the SVD.
D is wrong: Cholesky uses L and its transpose.

questions.q: What is the singular value decomposition?
options: A = U Σ Vᵀ, with orthogonal U, V and non-negative singular values on Σ
A = X Λ X⁻¹ for every matrix
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.6: It exists for every m × n matrix.
A is wrong: That is elimination.
C is wrong: That is Gram-Schmidt.
D is wrong: Not every matrix is diagonalisable.

questions.q: How are singular values related to AᵀA?
options: They equal the eigenvalues of A
They equal the diagonal of A
They are the pivots of A
Their squares are the eigenvalues of AᵀA
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.8: The right singular vectors are the eigenvectors of AᵀA.
A is wrong: Not in general.
B is wrong: Not in general.
C is wrong: Pivots are different.

questions.q: What does the Eckart-Young theorem say?
options: Keeping the first k rank-one pieces of the SVD gives the best rank-k approximation
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.9: If singular values fall off quickly, few pieces suffice.
A is wrong: Rank varies.
C is wrong: That is the product rule.
D is wrong: That is a different fact.

questions.q: In PCA, what does the first left singular vector of the centred data matrix give?
options: The direction of greatest variation in the data
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.11: PCA reduces data to its dominant patterns.
B is wrong: The mean is subtracted first.
C is wrong: That is the last singular vector.
D is wrong: That is a count.
